sections.h: Atrahasis: plague and drought before the Flood
sections.b: The Babylonian poem Atrahasis sets the Flood at the end of a series of disasters. Within spans the poem counts in hundreds of years (600, then not yet 1,200), humankind grows, its "noise" keeps the god Enlil awake, and he sends something to cut it down: first a plague (Atrahasis 5:7-21), then a drought (Atrahasis 6:6-43), then famine (Tablet II), and only then the Flood. Tikva Frymer-Kensky reports that Anne Kilmer and William Moran argued that the gods' problem is overpopulation. Genesis begins with the same growth ("When humankind began to grow many," Genesis 6:1) but gives a moral cause: evil and violence (Genesis 6:5, 11). It has no rounds of plague before the Flood, only the 120 years of Genesis 6:3, which some have compared with the poem's 1,200 years (Millard 1967).

common: Atrahasis and Genesis 6 both begin the Flood story with humankind growing in number.
uncommon: A. R. Millard (1967) held that, though an equation of the "din" with the violence of Genesis 6 "may appear improbable," the idea of humankind disturbing heaven is common to Atrahasis and Genesis 6.

sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis the hero first appears during the plague: "his god was Enki; his ear was open. He spoke with his god, and his god, in turn, spoke with him" (Atrahasis 5:23-25). He is Enki's "servant," obeys his god's instructions to the letter, and has the rank to gather the elders (Atrahasis 5:35, 5:48-49); one copy calls him "the sage" (Atrahasis 6:57). A. R. Millard (1967) held that Atrahasis and Genesis "undoubtedly describe the same Flood," and that the name may mean "exceedingly devout" as well as "exceedingly wise." Genesis praises Noah for something else: "Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his generations. Noah walked with God" (Genesis 6:9), and "He did everything just as God commanded him" (Genesis 6:22).

claude.title: A herald, then and now
claude.body: My own observation. Atrahasis's first act in the poem is to send out heralds (Atrahasis 5:38, 5:67), with a message to stop worshiping the gods and bribe the plague god. 2 Peter calls Noah "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5). If both remember one man, the Bible keeps the memory of a preacher; the Babylonian poem, of a clever man who knew how to work the gods.

sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis the god Enlil adds childlessness to a drought on purpose: "Let the womb be tied shut, so it brings no baby out safely" (Atrahasis 6:31), and the plain "gives birth" to salt (Atrahasis 6:27). The aim is fewer people. In the same poem the birth goddesses, not one God, open the womb (Atrahasis 4:28). The Bible gives the opening and closing of wombs to God alone (Genesis 20:18; 29:31; 30:22; 1 Samuel 1:5), and his settled purpose is life: "Would I, who bring to birth, shut the womb?" (Isaiah 66:9).
sections.refs: Atrahasis 4:28; Atrahasis 6:27-31; Genesis 20:17-18; Genesis 29:31; Genesis 30:22; 1 Samuel 1:5; Isaiah 66:9

sections.h: Marriage decreed by a goddess: Atrahasis
sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis, after the first people are made, the mother goddess Mami lays down how they will grow up and marry: the young man lifts his eyes to the young woman, and "Out in the orchards and the lanes, let a wife and her husband pick each other" (Atrahasis 4:21-22). Weddings last nine days, in honor of Ishtar, goddess of love (Atrahasis 4:49-52). Genesis also moves from the making of male and female to marriage (Genesis 1:27; 2:24), but there marriage is God's own gift and joining, as Jesus says: "What God has yoked together, then, no human being should separate" (Matthew 19:6).

sections.h: Adad holds back the rain: Atrahasis
sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis the god Enlil orders the storm god Adad, the Hadad of Syria, to hold back his rain: "Let Adad keep back his rain ... Let the clouds grow thick, but let no drop fall" (Atrahasis 6:13, 6:18-19). The drought is meant to starve humankind into silence. The Bible's drought stories answer the belief that the storm god controls rain: Elijah declares, "these coming years will have no dew and no rain unless I give the word" (1 Kings 17:1), and the rain returns when the LORD answers on Carmel.

In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis, Enlil, ruler of the earth, cannot act alone. Twice he calls the great gods together and asks their consent for a plague and a drought against humankind (Atrahasis 5:6-15; 6:5-31). The Nineveh copies call them "the gods, his sons." In the council the gods argue, and Enki works against Enlil's plans. The Bible's council pictures are different: one God presides and judges the rest (Psalm 82:1; 1 Kings 22:19; Job 1:6).

sections.h: Atrahasis: humans take up the gods' tools
sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis the gods burned their tools in a strike (Atrahasis 2:28-30), and humankind was made to do their work. After the first births the new people "made hoes and spades anew" and "built large dikes" for the people's food and, it seems, the gods' (Atrahasis 4:67-69). Genesis also gives work from the start, "to work it and to guard it" (Genesis 2:15), but as a calling in God's garden, not a burden passed down from the gods; toil comes after the curse (Genesis 3:17-19), and the Sabbath and Christ's call to rest set limits on it (Matthew 11:28).
sections.refs: Atrahasis 2:28-30; Atrahasis 4:67-69; Genesis 2:15; Genesis 3:17-19; Genesis 4:22; Matthew 11:28

sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis the god Enki tells humankind to stop worshiping their own gods and bring all their bread and flour offerings to Namtar, the god of the plague, "Let the gifts put him to shame, and let him pass his hand over them" (Atrahasis 5:40-47). The elders build Namtar a house and the plague ends (Atrahasis 5:64-77). The Bible says the LORD "does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17), and it reads offerings to the gods of the nations as offerings to demons (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20) or to nothing (Psalm 115:4-7).

sections.h: A god who cannot sleep: Atrahasis
sections.b: In the Babylonian poem Atrahasis the god Enlil complains, "Their uproar robs me of sleep" (Atrahasis 5:10; 6:10), and sends plague and drought to quiet humankind. Another god, Enki, works against him. The Bible answers both pictures: Israel's guard "does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4), and because God is one, judgment and healing come from the same hand: "it was he who tore us apart, and he will heal us" (Hosea 6:1).
